title: Three.js versus Game Engine
author: BrotherMoy
selftext:
Hello everyone. I just thought I'd post this because it feels like too many people are confused about this.

When making 3D games, you need to render the graphics. Three.js is a JavaScript library that allows rendering 3D graphics in the browser. Game engines have built in renderers that usually come with more integrated features. 

Why does AI prefer Three.js?

When you ask AI to make or prototype a game, it has no access to a game engine right out of the box. To have AI use the game engine, you have to download a game engine and connect it to your AI in some way (either via MCP or just directly to files). However, AI can use Three.js directly in your chat with no installations because they have built in web environments. This is why an AI will usually suggest using Three.js because the set up is instant.

Which is better?

In my opinion, using a game engine is much better than Three.js because Three.js is simply a renderer and a game engine has audio, physics, UI, etc. that now has to be built from scratch on top of the rendering if you are using Three.js. That being said, this used to be a bigger problem when AI wasn't as capable. Nowadays, AI can build an audio system, physics system, and any other system you want on top of your Three.js renderer. Hell it can even build an entire engine with a renderer from scratch. It also used to be that game engines could easily port your games to different systems and consoles much easier than AI. But now, you can just ask AI to port your browser game to mobile and it will pretty easily create a mobile wrapper for your game.

I would say for very low level beginners, and very high level experts, having AI build everything from scratch is a benefit to you. A beginner doesn't know how to navigate an engine so they don't care as long as the game is working, and an expert can now build their perfect custom engine exactly as they want with the help of AI. A mid level developer (which I think is the average) would benefit more from using a game engine that already has a lot of features out of the box, and they can use the editor to tweak things without asking AI for something stupid like "change sprint speed". 

I hope this helps somebody trying to figure out what to use or wondering why people use different solutions.

TLDR: Three.js is just a renderer that AI can use for immediate prototyping, and game engines have a lot more features than just rendering but require more setup for AI to use

replies.author: FragmentedHeap
replies.body:
Not that user, but I've basically done the same thing.

The process I took was getting as modular as possible and thinking about all the pieces I need for a custom app/game engine where my primary requirement was cross platform on linux/windows/mac with no exceptions.

And I broke it down into individual modular git repos

\* Text Rendering  
\* Audio  
\* Window Management  
\* Graphics API  
\* Images  
\* Video  
\* 2d Layout (ui stuff)  
\* 3d world/engine (this is where the engine components come in)

I built a text rendering engine from scratch, because I wanted MTSDF (multi channel signed distance field) font rendering as a native feature without doing traditional text rendering or raster techniques.  And I wanted it to work by enabling you to compile normal fonts into MTSDF fonts as a binary format instead of json atlas maps.  So I designed all that, and had AI build it, using many academic papers for input and someone's college thesis on it.  It works, very well, and I got it to be really efficient for what it's doing.

So now I can render sharp text at any scale on just about any surface.  I can render text on water... I can render the WHOLE user interface on water, or in the air, or on a door, or w/e. I can put UI on ANYTHING.

Once that was good I built a full audio suite, many rust crates, one repo, many crates.

And then I did Winit for window management.

And then I did a repo for images "tessera" that supports basically every image format, even hdr and tiff etc, svg too of course

And video with most sensible video codecs

and then 2d layout (origami) I designed as an extremely gutted web like Layout engine using taffy from rust, with a real css engine for styling, but it ships NO ELEMENTS.  I made all the elements a separate crate, like origimai-html and it's optional.  You can implement your own elements and orgiami extends the css with them and you can style them with the same css engine.

if you use the html crate, you get most web elements, and you get a subset of HTML and can degine a UI in that html/css, but all the code is server side, there's no Javascript, and no "client side"

Now I'm working on the content/asset pipeline so HTML can be hot loaded etc and or precompiled.

I will keep going until the engine is done and I can make apps or games with it.

It's all on web gpu, but it has escape hatches so you can get to the backend (vulkan, directx, metal, etc).

I have AI work on 1 piece, one module, and they all hook up as one system.

Heres the LAB running,

And yeah, everything generates charp bindings and capi dlls, and fully supports c# on .net 11 with runtime async features that just came out days ago.  I already moved it to .net 11.

The core is built in rust, and I made csharp a first class feature.  But I might add a js engine later, and I might support python and even having embeded cypthon and letting the engine directly run python.  I doubt I will support Java any time soon.  But Csharp, definitely. That's my jam, 23+ years .net dev...

Everything you see in this screen shot, is from scratch in rust/csharp, even the text rendering engine, nothing on the screen wasn't built from the ground up.

Now I leaned on a lot of open source stuff, mit projects, popular sound libraries, image stuff, etc, but I'm rolling it all together into one platform.

Text is from scratch, mtsdf, but it does use some hinting libraries etc from freetype techniques, so the text looks good even when it's really small.

My goal is to make UI so good in a game that you can render UI's on objects in the game almost effortlessly and interact with them in the game as they are rendered in the world.

replies.author: BrotherMoy
replies.body: Honest question, do you recommend someone like me who has dabbled in game engines to create systems from scratch? How should I go about doing this when my typical approach is to prototype gameplay/mechanics and then just build the environments using native lightings and material rendering

replies.author: Internal-Capital7471
replies.body:
I don't recommend to just do it with no guidance. You do need to have a pretty solid understanding of how things work, so you can identify what's wrong and where to improve. So many of these vibecoded game creators are incapable of identifying where they are lacking--so many of them perform absolutely terribly, and the vibecoders themselves lack the background knowledge to know what to even be asking their ai agents to do in the first place.

I do recommend that you make systems from scratch, but I'd first recommend that you understand the systems you are building too. Thankfully, AI is extremely good as a teaching tool too, and you can learn just by asking.

One thing I would recommend you do is that when you make a new system, ask AI to research all of the best practices on the system you're planning to make, and make a plan to design it. This is a standing rule in my workflow, although I've done lots of graphics programming there's still a ton of systems I don't know so I have AI prep itself to make them.

replies.author: Internal-Capital7471
replies.body:
I've been doing indie game deving (actually more like indie graphics programming) for a very long time, always trying to optimize games, so I learned well how game engines work and how the graphics pipeline works.

Staying with a game engine limits you to the engine, and makes your AI want to stay in that limited scope. Playing with different rendering systems and exploring outside that constraint is really beneficial. For instance, my AI has been optimizing my game, and has discovered that if we do a pass on all pixels on the screen, and group them into different types, we can optimize our shaders heavily by not including extraneous information in them. Might sound odd, but with all the procedural graphics there's a ton of  stuff in the shaders that we don't need per pixel, and mobile is even more limited in this area.

I still have lots to go, but this is a screenshot of what we currently have. I'm working now on the water shader, the reflections. Next, I think I'm going to tackle better texturing in general like on the mountains, and then using rock-ledge prefabs to decorate the rims much like Skyrim does.

https://i.redd.it/ltuuezhm121i1.png

replies.author: BrotherMoy
replies.body: Like I told the other guy, this is impressive and definitely a scenario where somebody who is more advanced (I said expert in my post) would rather create an engine from scratch. I think the average game developer or person who has dabbled in game dev before would benefit from an engine because creating any system from scratch is just extra work. If my goal is to make a fun game, most game engines can achieve that with little bottlenecks. But if my goal is to do something very specific with rendering, or audio, or text rendering (like the other guy), then I need to create things from scratch

replies.author: Internal-Capital7471
replies.body:
if you're looking at an art pipeline you can control, you need to build your art out of constructed pieces so you can control it deliberately. It isn't any use to just prompt your AI to make it look a little different, you need a blueprint of how your character is constructed.

An easy way to make consistent 2d art is using 3d pieces and rendering it into a lower resolution with effects. The specific process varies, but you can ask AI to learn how to do it. 

If you keep prompting AI to make little changes here and there but you don't have a concrete way of expressing your art, you are not going to have much control over it.
